title: Budgeted Multi-Source Counterfactual Annotation for Off-Policy Evaluation
claim: Annotation sources help or harm depending on their error regime, via distinct effects on bias and variance components of error.
layout: 4 panels in a row, shared x-axis, color-coded legend on top
description: A single horizontal strip of four line plots sharing the x-axis, number of annotations from 0 to 1000. A legend across the top names four annotation sources in green, orange, blue and red, each labeled with a regime from always beneficial to always harmful. The panels are titled Scaled MSE, J1 (Bias Pollution), J2 (Bias Correction) and J3 (Reward Variance). Each panel shows mean curves with translucent shaded bands for one standard deviation. In Scaled MSE, the green curve falls while the red curve rises and then plateaus. In J1 and J2, the red and blue curves climb steeply, while the green and orange curves stay flat and low. In J3, green and blue fall while orange and red first rise and then decline. The bands overlap heavily. The eye goes first to the diverging curves in the leftmost panel.
caption: Scaled mean squared error (MSE) $\mathcal V$ and the allocation-dependent components $J_1$, $J_2$, and $J_3$ versus the number of annotations for the four annotation sources in Table [ref]. Shaded bands show $\pm 1$ standard deviation over $100$ environments.
abstract: Off-policy evaluation (OPE) estimates the value of a target policy from logged data, but limited behavior-policy coverage can force high-variance reweighting or reward-model extrapolation. Counterfactual annotations can add evidence about unobserved actions, yet practical sources, including domain experts and large language models (LLMs), may be costly, biased, or noisy. We study budgeted acquisition of such annotations for contextual-bandit OPE. Given source-specific costs and error profiles, we formulate an integer allocation problem over context-action pairs and annotation sources to minimize the component of estimator variance that depends on the annotation plan. We characterize when annotations are valuable through a first-annotation threshold and local annotation-value regimes. For the coupled multi-source problem, we develop a majorization-minimization algorithm with dynamic-programming subroutines that monotonically improves the objective. Experiments in synthetic clinical and LLM-annotated education bandits show that our allocation method reduces fixed-profile mean squared error (MSE) by 20.58% and 10.77%, respectively, relative to no annotation.
